lines: Peace, ho! Hear Antony; most noble Antony.

speeches.speaker: ANTONY
lines: Why, friends, you go to do you know not what.
Wherein hath Caesar thus deserved your loves?
Alas, you know not; I must tell you then.
You have forgot the will I told you of.

speeches.speaker: CITIZENS
lines: Most true; the will!—let’s stay, and hear the will.

speeches.speaker: ANTONY
lines: Here is the will, and under Caesar’s seal.
To every Roman citizen he gives,
To every several man, seventy-five drachmas.

speeches.speaker: SECOND CITIZEN
lines: Most noble Caesar! We’ll revenge his death.

speeches.speaker: THIRD CITIZEN
lines: O, royal Caesar!

speeches.speaker: ANTONY
lines: Hear me with patience.

speeches.speaker: CITIZENS
lines: Peace, ho!

speeches.speaker: ANTONY
lines: Moreover, he hath left you all his walks,
His private arbors, and new-planted orchards,
On this side Tiber; he hath left them you,
And to your heirs forever; common pleasures,
To walk abroad, and recreate yourselves.
Here was a Caesar! when comes such another?

speeches.speaker: FIRST CITIZEN
lines: Never, never. Come, away, away!
We’ll burn his body in the holy place,
And with the brands fire the traitors’ houses.
Take up the body.

speeches.speaker: SECOND CITIZEN
lines: Go, fetch fire.

speeches.speaker: THIRD CITIZEN
lines: Pluck down benches.

speeches.speaker: FOURTH CITIZEN
lines: Pluck down forms, windows, anything.

speeches.speaker: ANTONY
lines: Now let it work. Mischief, thou art afoot,
Take thou what course thou wilt!

speeches.speaker: SERVANT
lines: Sir, Octavius is already come to Rome.

speeches.speaker: ANTONY
lines: Where is he?

speeches.speaker: SERVANT
lines: He and Lepidus are at Caesar’s house.

speeches.speaker: ANTONY
lines: And thither will I straight to visit him.
He comes upon a wish. Fortune is merry,
And in this mood will give us anything.

speeches.speaker: SERVANT
lines: I heard him say Brutus and Cassius
Are rid like madmen through the gates of Rome.

speeches.speaker: ANTONY
lines: Belike they had some notice of the people,
How I had moved them. Bring me to Octavius.

speeches.stage: Enter Cinna, the poet, and after him the citizens.

speeches.speaker: CINNA
lines: I dreamt tonight that I did feast with Caesar,
And things unluckily charge my fantasy.
I have no will to wander forth of doors,
Yet something leads me forth.

speeches.speaker: FIRST CITIZEN
lines: What is your name?

speeches.speaker: SECOND CITIZEN
lines: Whither are you going?

speeches.speaker: THIRD CITIZEN
lines: Where do you dwell?

speeches.speaker: FOURTH CITIZEN
lines: Are you a married man or a bachelor?

speeches.speaker: SECOND CITIZEN
lines: Answer every man directly.

speeches.speaker: FIRST CITIZEN
lines: Ay, and briefly.

speeches.speaker: FOURTH CITIZEN
lines: Ay, and wisely.

speeches.speaker: THIRD CITIZEN
lines: Ay, and truly, you were best.

speeches.speaker: CINNA
lines: What is my name? Whither am I going? Where do I dwell? Am I a married
man or a bachelor? Then, to answer every man directly and briefly,
wisely and truly. Wisely I say I am a bachelor.

speeches.speaker: SECOND CITIZEN
lines: That’s as much as to say they are fools that marry; you’ll bear me a
bang for that, I fear. Proceed, directly.

speeches.speaker: CINNA
lines: Directly, I am going to Caesar’s funeral.

speeches.speaker: FIRST CITIZEN
lines: As a friend, or an enemy?

speeches.speaker: CINNA
lines: As a friend.

speeches.speaker: SECOND CITIZEN
lines: That matter is answered directly.

speeches.speaker: FOURTH CITIZEN
lines: For your dwelling, briefly.

speeches.speaker: CINNA
lines: Briefly, I dwell by the Capitol.

speeches.speaker: THIRD CITIZEN
lines: Your name, sir, truly.

speeches.speaker: CINNA
lines: Truly, my name is Cinna.

speeches.speaker: FIRST CITIZEN
lines: Tear him to pieces! He’s a conspirator.

speeches.speaker: CINNA
lines: I am Cinna the poet, I am Cinna the poet.

speeches.speaker: FOURTH CITIZEN
lines: Tear him for his bad verses, tear him for his bad verses.

speeches.speaker: CINNA
lines: I am not Cinna the conspirator.

speeches.speaker: FOURTH CITIZEN
lines: It is no matter, his name’s Cinna; pluck but his name out of his heart,
and turn him going.

speeches.speaker: THIRD CITIZEN
lines: Tear him, tear him! Come; brands, ho! firebrands. To Brutus’, to
Cassius’; burn all. Some to Decius’ house, and some to Casca’s, some to
Ligarius’. Away, go!

scenes.setting: Rome. A room in Antony’s house

speeches.stage: Enter Antony, Octavius and Lepidus, seated at a table.

speeches.speaker: ANTONY
lines: These many then shall die; their names are prick’d.

speeches.speaker: OCTAVIUS
lines: Your brother too must die; consent you, Lepidus?

speeches.speaker: LEPIDUS
lines: I do consent,—

speeches.speaker: OCTAVIUS
lines: Prick him down, Antony.

speeches.speaker: LEPIDUS
lines: Upon condition Publius shall not live,
Who is your sister’s son, Mark Antony.

speeches.speaker: ANTONY
lines: He shall not live; look, with a spot I damn him.
But, Lepidus, go you to Caesar’s house;
Fetch the will hither, and we shall determine
How to cut off some charge in legacies.

speeches.speaker: LEPIDUS
lines: What, shall I find you here?

speeches.speaker: OCTAVIUS
lines: Or here, or at the Capitol.

speeches.speaker: ANTONY
lines: This is a slight unmeritable man,
Meet to be sent on errands. Is it fit,
The three-fold world divided, he should stand
One of the three to share it?

speeches.speaker: OCTAVIUS
lines: So you thought him,
And took his voice who should be prick’d to die
In our black sentence and proscription.

speeches.speaker: ANTONY
lines: Octavius, I have seen more days than you;
And though we lay these honours on this man,
To ease ourselves of divers sland’rous loads,
He shall but bear them as the ass bears gold,
To groan and sweat under the business,
Either led or driven, as we point the way;
And having brought our treasure where we will,
Then take we down his load, and turn him off,
Like to the empty ass, to shake his ears,
And graze in commons.

speeches.speaker: OCTAVIUS
lines: You may do your will;
But he’s a tried and valiant soldier.

speeches.speaker: ANTONY
lines: So is my horse, Octavius; and for that
I do appoint him store of provender.
It is a creature that I teach to fight,
To wind, to stop, to run directly on,
His corporal motion govern’d by my spirit.
And, in some taste, is Lepidus but so:
He must be taught, and train’d, and bid go forth:
A barren-spirited fellow; one that feeds
On objects, arts, and imitations,
Which, out of use and stal’d by other men,
Begin his fashion. Do not talk of him
But as a property. And now, Octavius,
Listen great things. Brutus and Cassius
Are levying powers; we must straight make head.
Therefore let our alliance be combin’d,
Our best friends made, our means stretch’d;
And let us presently go sit in council,
How covert matters may be best disclos’d,
And open perils surest answered.

speeches.speaker: OCTAVIUS
lines: Let us do so: for we are at the stake,
And bay’d about with many enemies;
And some that smile have in their hearts, I fear,
Millions of mischiefs.

scenes.setting: Before Brutus’ tent, in the camp near Sardis

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Stand, ho!

speeches.speaker: LUCILIUS
lines: Give the word, ho! and stand.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: What now, Lucilius! is Cassius near?

speeches.speaker: LUCILIUS
lines: He is at hand, and Pindarus is come
To do you salutation from his master.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: He greets me well. Your master, Pindarus,
In his own change, or by ill officers,
Hath given me some worthy cause to wish
Things done, undone: but, if he be at hand,
I shall be satisfied.

speeches.speaker: PINDARUS
lines: I do not doubt
But that my noble master will appear
Such as he is, full of regard and honour.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: He is not doubted. A word, Lucilius;
How he received you, let me be resolv’d.

speeches.speaker: LUCILIUS
lines: With courtesy and with respect enough,
But not with such familiar instances,
Nor with such free and friendly conference,
As he hath us’d of old.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Thou hast describ’d
A hot friend cooling. Ever note, Lucilius,
When love begins to sicken and decay
It useth an enforced ceremony.
There are no tricks in plain and simple faith;
But hollow men, like horses hot at hand,
Make gallant show and promise of their mettle;

speeches.speaker: LUCILIUS
lines: They meant this night in Sardis to be quarter’d;
The greater part, the horse in general,
Are come with Cassius.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Hark! he is arriv’d.
March gently on to meet him.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: Stand, ho!

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Stand, ho! Speak the word along.

speeches.speaker: FIRST SOLDIER
lines: Stand!

speeches.speaker: SECOND SOLDIER
lines: Stand!

speeches.speaker: THIRD SOLDIER
lines: Stand!

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: Most noble brother, you have done me wrong.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Judge me, you gods; wrong I mine enemies?
And if not so, how should I wrong a brother?

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: Brutus, this sober form of yours hides wrongs;
And when you do them—

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Cassius, be content.
Speak your griefs softly, I do know you well.
Before the eyes of both our armies here,
Which should perceive nothing but love from us,
Let us not wrangle. Bid them move away;
Then in my tent, Cassius, enlarge your griefs,
And I will give you audience.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: Pindarus,
Bid our commanders lead their charges off
A little from this ground.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Lucilius, do you the like; and let no man
Come to our tent till we have done our conference.
Lucius and Titinius, guard our door.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: That you have wrong’d me doth appear in this:
You have condemn’d and noted Lucius Pella
For taking bribes here of the Sardians;
Wherein my letters, praying on his side
Because I knew the man, were slighted off.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: You wrong’d yourself to write in such a case.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: In such a time as this it is not meet
That every nice offence should bear his comment.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Let me tell you, Cassius, you yourself
Are much condemn’d to have an itching palm,
To sell and mart your offices for gold
To undeservers.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: I an itching palm!
You know that you are Brutus that speak this,
Or, by the gods, this speech were else your last.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: The name of Cassius honours this corruption,
And chastisement doth therefore hide his head.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: Chastisement!

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Remember March, the Ides of March remember:
Did not great Julius bleed for justice’ sake?
What villain touch’d his body, that did stab,
And not for justice? What! Shall one of us,
That struck the foremost man of all this world
But for supporting robbers, shall we now
Contaminate our fingers with base bribes,
And sell the mighty space of our large honours
For so much trash as may be grasped thus?
I had rather be a dog, and bay the moon,
Than such a Roman.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: Brutus, bait not me,
I’ll not endure it. You forget yourself,
To hedge me in. I am a soldier, I,
Older in practice, abler than yourself
To make conditions.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Go to; you are not, Cassius.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: I am.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: I say you are not.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: Urge me no more, I shall forget myself;
Have mind upon your health, tempt me no farther.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Away, slight man!

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: Is’t possible?

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Hear me, for I will speak.
Must I give way and room to your rash choler?
Shall I be frighted when a madman stares?

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: O ye gods, ye gods! Must I endure all this?

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: All this? ay, more: fret till your proud heart break;
Go show your slaves how choleric you are,
And make your bondmen tremble. Must I budge?
Must I observe you? Must I stand and crouch
Under your testy humour? By the gods,
You shall digest the venom of your spleen,
Though it do split you; for, from this day forth,
I’ll use you for my mirth, yea, for my laughter,
When you are waspish.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: Is it come to this?

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: You say you are a better soldier:
Let it appear so; make your vaunting true,
And it shall please me well. For mine own part,
I shall be glad to learn of noble men.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: You wrong me every way, you wrong me, Brutus.
I said, an elder soldier, not a better:
Did I say better?

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: If you did, I care not.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: When Caesar liv’d, he durst not thus have mov’d me.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Peace, peace! you durst not so have tempted him.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: I durst not?

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: No.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: What? durst not tempt him?

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: For your life you durst not.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: Do not presume too much upon my love.
I may do that I shall be sorry for.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: You have done that you should be sorry for.
There is no terror, Cassius, in your threats,
For I am arm’d so strong in honesty,
That they pass by me as the idle wind,
Which I respect not. I did send to you
For certain sums of gold, which you denied me;
For I can raise no money by vile means:
By Heaven, I had rather coin my heart,
And drop my blood for drachmas, than to wring
From the hard hands of peasants their vile trash
By any indirection. I did send
To you for gold to pay my legions,
Which you denied me: was that done like Cassius?
Should I have answer’d Caius Cassius so?
When Marcus Brutus grows so covetous,
To lock such rascal counters from his friends,
Be ready, gods, with all your thunderbolts,
Dash him to pieces!

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: I denied you not.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: You did.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: I did not. He was but a fool
That brought my answer back. Brutus hath riv’d my heart.
A friend should bear his friend’s infirmities;
But Brutus makes mine greater than they are.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: I do not, till you practise them on me.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: You love me not.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: I do not like your faults.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: A friendly eye could never see such faults.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: A flatterer’s would not, though they do appear
As huge as high Olympus.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: Come, Antony, and young Octavius, come,
Revenge yourselves alone on Cassius,
For Cassius is a-weary of the world:
Hated by one he loves; brav’d by his brother;
Check’d like a bondman; all his faults observ’d,
Set in a note-book, learn’d and conn’d by rote,
To cast into my teeth. O, I could weep
My spirit from mine eyes! There is my dagger,
And here my naked breast; within, a heart
Dearer than Plutus’ mine, richer than gold:
If that thou be’st a Roman, take it forth.
I, that denied thee gold, will give my heart:
Strike as thou didst at Caesar; for I know,
When thou didst hate him worst, thou lovedst him better
Than ever thou lovedst Cassius.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Sheathe your dagger.
Be angry when you will, it shall have scope;
Do what you will, dishonour shall be humour.
O Cassius, you are yoked with a lamb
That carries anger as the flint bears fire,
Who, much enforced, shows a hasty spark,
And straight is cold again.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: Hath Cassius liv’d
To be but mirth and laughter to his Brutus,
When grief and blood ill-temper’d vexeth him?

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: When I spoke that, I was ill-temper’d too.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: Do you confess so much? Give me your hand.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: And my heart too.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: O Brutus!

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: What’s the matter?

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: Have not you love enough to bear with me,
When that rash humour which my mother gave me
Makes me forgetful?

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Yes, Cassius; and from henceforth,
When you are over-earnest with your Brutus,
He’ll think your mother chides, and leave you so.

speeches.stage: Enter Poet, followed by Lucilius, Titinius and Lucius.

speeches.speaker: POET
lines: There is some grudge between ’em; ’tis not meet
They be alone.
speeches.stage: [_Within._] Let me go in to see the generals,

speeches.speaker: LUCILIUS
speeches.stage: [_Within._] You shall not come to them.

speeches.speaker: POET
speeches.stage: [_Within._] Nothing but death shall stay me.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: How now! What’s the matter?

speeches.speaker: POET
lines: For shame, you generals! What do you mean?
Love, and be friends, as two such men should be;
For I have seen more years, I’m sure, than ye.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: Ha, ha! How vilely doth this cynic rhyme!

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Get you hence, sirrah. Saucy fellow, hence!

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: Bear with him, Brutus; ’tis his fashion.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: I’ll know his humour when he knows his time.
What should the wars do with these jigging fools?
Companion, hence!

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: Away, away, be gone!

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Lucilius and Titinius, bid the commanders
Prepare to lodge their companies tonight.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: And come yourselves and bring Messala with you
Immediately to us.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Lucius, a bowl of wine.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: I did not think you could have been so angry.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: O Cassius, I am sick of many griefs.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: Of your philosophy you make no use,
If you give place to accidental evils.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: No man bears sorrow better. Portia is dead.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: Ha? Portia?

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: She is dead.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: How ’scap’d I killing, when I cross’d you so?
O insupportable and touching loss!
Upon what sickness?

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Impatient of my absence,
And grief that young Octavius with Mark Antony
Have made themselves so strong; for with her death
That tidings came. With this she fell distract,
And, her attendants absent, swallow’d fire.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: And died so?

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Even so.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: O ye immortal gods!

speeches.stage: Enter Lucius, with wine and a taper.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Speak no more of her. Give me a bowl of wine.
In this I bury all unkindness, Cassius.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: My heart is thirsty for that noble pledge.
Fill, Lucius, till the wine o’erswell the cup.
I cannot drink too much of Brutus’ love.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Come in, Titinius!
Welcome, good Messala.
Now sit we close about this taper here,
And call in question our necessities.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: Portia, art thou gone?

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: No more, I pray you.
Messala, I have here received letters,
That young Octavius and Mark Antony
Come down upon us with a mighty power,
Bending their expedition toward Philippi.

speeches.speaker: MESSALA
lines: Myself have letters of the selfsame tenor.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: With what addition?

speeches.speaker: MESSALA
lines: That by proscription and bills of outlawry
Octavius, Antony, and Lepidus
Have put to death an hundred Senators.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Therein our letters do not well agree.
Mine speak of seventy Senators that died
By their proscriptions, Cicero being one.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: Cicero one!

speeches.speaker: MESSALA
lines: Cicero is dead,
And by that order of proscription.
Had you your letters from your wife, my lord?

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: No, Messala.

speeches.speaker: MESSALA
lines: Nor nothing in your letters writ of her?

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Nothing, Messala.

speeches.speaker: MESSALA
lines: That, methinks, is strange.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Why ask you? Hear you aught of her in yours?

speeches.speaker: MESSALA
lines: No, my lord.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Now as you are a Roman, tell me true.

speeches.speaker: MESSALA
lines: Then like a Roman bear the truth I tell,
For certain she is dead, and by strange manner.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Why, farewell, Portia. We must die, Messala.
With meditating that she must die once,
I have the patience to endure it now.

speeches.speaker: MESSALA
lines: Even so great men great losses should endure.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: I have as much of this in art as you,
But yet my nature could not bear it so.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Well, to our work alive. What do you think
Of marching to Philippi presently?

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: I do not think it good.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Your reason?

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: This it is:
’Tis better that the enemy seek us;
So shall he waste his means, weary his soldiers,
Doing himself offence, whilst we, lying still,
Are full of rest, defence, and nimbleness.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Good reasons must of force give place to better.
The people ’twixt Philippi and this ground
Do stand but in a forced affection;
For they have grudg’d us contribution.
The enemy, marching along by them,
By them shall make a fuller number up,
Come on refresh’d, new-added, and encourag’d;
From which advantage shall we cut him off
If at Philippi we do face him there,
These people at our back.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: Hear me, good brother.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Under your pardon. You must note besides,
That we have tried the utmost of our friends,
Our legions are brim-full, our cause is ripe.
The enemy increaseth every day;
We, at the height, are ready to decline.
There is a tide in the affairs of men,
Which, taken at the flood, leads on to fortune;
Omitted, all the voyage of their life
Is bound in shallows and in miseries.
On such a full sea are we now afloat,
And we must take the current when it serves,
Or lose our ventures.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: Then, with your will, go on:
We’ll along ourselves, and meet them at Philippi.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: The deep of night is crept upon our talk,
And nature must obey necessity,
Which we will niggard with a little rest.
There is no more to say?

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: No more. Good night:
Early tomorrow will we rise, and hence.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Lucius! My gown.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: O my dear brother!
This was an ill beginning of the night.
Never come such division ’tween our souls!
Let it not, Brutus.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Everything is well.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: Good night, my lord.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Good night, good brother.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Farewell, everyone.

speeches.speaker: LUCIUS
lines: Here in the tent.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: What, thou speak’st drowsily?
Poor knave, I blame thee not, thou art o’er-watch’d.
Call Claudius and some other of my men;
I’ll have them sleep on cushions in my tent.

speeches.speaker: LUCIUS
lines: Varro and Claudius!

speeches.speaker: VARRO
lines: Calls my lord?

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: I pray you, sirs, lie in my tent and sleep;
It may be I shall raise you by-and-by
On business to my brother Cassius.

speeches.speaker: VARRO
lines: So please you, we will stand and watch your pleasure.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: I will not have it so; lie down, good sirs,
It may be I shall otherwise bethink me.
Look, Lucius, here’s the book I sought for so;
I put it in the pocket of my gown.

speeches.speaker: LUCIUS
lines: I was sure your lordship did not give it me.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Bear with me, good boy, I am much forgetful.
Canst thou hold up thy heavy eyes awhile,
And touch thy instrument a strain or two?

speeches.speaker: LUCIUS
lines: Ay, my lord, an’t please you.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: It does, my boy.
I trouble thee too much, but thou art willing.

speeches.speaker: LUCIUS
lines: It is my duty, sir.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: I should not urge thy duty past thy might;
I know young bloods look for a time of rest.

speeches.speaker: LUCIUS
lines: I have slept, my lord, already.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: It was well done, and thou shalt sleep again;
I will not hold thee long. If I do live,
I will be good to thee.

speeches.stage: [_Lucius plays and sings till he falls asleep._]

speeches.speaker: GHOST
lines: Thy evil spirit, Brutus.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Why com’st thou?

speeches.speaker: GHOST
lines: To tell thee thou shalt see me at Philippi.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Well; then I shall see thee again?

speeches.speaker: GHOST
lines: Ay, at Philippi.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Why, I will see thee at Philippi then.

speeches.speaker: LUCIUS
lines: The strings, my lord, are false.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: He thinks he still is at his instrument.
Lucius, awake!

speeches.speaker: LUCIUS
lines: My lord?

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Didst thou dream, Lucius, that thou so criedst out?

speeches.speaker: LUCIUS
lines: My lord, I do not know that I did cry.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Yes, that thou didst. Didst thou see anything?

speeches.speaker: LUCIUS
lines: Nothing, my lord.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Sleep again, Lucius. Sirrah Claudius!
Fellow thou, awake!

speeches.speaker: VARRO
lines: My lord?

speeches.speaker: CLAUDIUS
lines: My lord?

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Why did you so cry out, sirs, in your sleep?

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Ay. Saw you anything?

speeches.speaker: VARRO
lines: No, my lord, I saw nothing.

speeches.speaker: CLAUDIUS
lines: Nor I, my lord.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Go and commend me to my brother Cassius;
Bid him set on his powers betimes before,
And we will follow.

speeches.stage: Enter Octavius, Antony and their Army.

speeches.speaker: OCTAVIUS
lines: Now, Antony, our hopes are answered.
You said the enemy would not come down,
But keep the hills and upper regions.
It proves not so; their battles are at hand,
They mean to warn us at Philippi here,
Answering before we do demand of them.

speeches.speaker: ANTONY
lines: Tut, I am in their bosoms, and I know
Wherefore they do it. They could be content
To visit other places, and come down
With fearful bravery, thinking by this face
To fasten in our thoughts that they have courage;
But ’tis not so.

speeches.speaker: MESSENGER
lines: Prepare you, generals.
The enemy comes on in gallant show;
Their bloody sign of battle is hung out,
And something to be done immediately.

speeches.speaker: ANTONY
lines: Octavius, lead your battle softly on
Upon the left hand of the even field.

speeches.speaker: OCTAVIUS
lines: Upon the right hand I. Keep thou the left.

speeches.speaker: ANTONY
lines: Why do you cross me in this exigent?

speeches.speaker: OCTAVIUS
lines: I do not cross you; but I will do so.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: They stand, and would have parley.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: Stand fast, Titinius; we must out and talk.

speeches.speaker: OCTAVIUS
lines: Mark Antony, shall we give sign of battle?

speeches.speaker: ANTONY
lines: No, Caesar, we will answer on their charge.
Make forth; the generals would have some words.

speeches.speaker: OCTAVIUS
lines: Stir not until the signal.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Words before blows: is it so, countrymen?

speeches.speaker: OCTAVIUS
lines: Not that we love words better, as you do.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Good words are better than bad strokes, Octavius.

speeches.speaker: ANTONY
lines: In your bad strokes, Brutus, you give good words;
Witness the hole you made in Caesar’s heart,
Crying, “Long live! Hail, Caesar!”

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: Antony,
The posture of your blows are yet unknown;
But for your words, they rob the Hybla bees,
And leave them honeyless.

speeches.speaker: ANTONY
lines: Not stingless too.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: O yes, and soundless too,
For you have stol’n their buzzing, Antony,
And very wisely threat before you sting.

speeches.speaker: ANTONY
lines: Villains, you did not so when your vile daggers
Hack’d one another in the sides of Caesar:
You show’d your teeth like apes, and fawn’d like hounds,
And bow’d like bondmen, kissing Caesar’s feet;
Whilst damned Casca, like a cur, behind
Struck Caesar on the neck. O you flatterers!

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: Flatterers! Now, Brutus, thank yourself.
This tongue had not offended so today,
If Cassius might have rul’d.

speeches.speaker: OCTAVIUS
lines: Come, come, the cause. If arguing makes us sweat,
The proof of it will turn to redder drops.
Look, I draw a sword against conspirators.
When think you that the sword goes up again?
Never, till Caesar’s three and thirty wounds
Be well aveng’d; or till another Caesar
Have added slaughter to the sword of traitors.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Caesar, thou canst not die by traitors’ hands,
Unless thou bring’st them with thee.

speeches.speaker: OCTAVIUS
lines: So I hope.
I was not born to die on Brutus’ sword.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: O, if thou wert the noblest of thy strain,
Young man, thou couldst not die more honourable.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: A peevish school-boy, worthless of such honour,
Join’d with a masker and a reveller.

speeches.speaker: ANTONY
lines: Old Cassius still!

speeches.speaker: OCTAVIUS
lines: Come, Antony; away!
Defiance, traitors, hurl we in your teeth.
If you dare fight today, come to the field;
If not, when you have stomachs.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: Why now, blow wind, swell billow, and swim bark!
The storm is up, and all is on the hazard.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Ho, Lucilius! Hark, a word with you.

speeches.speaker: LUCILIUS
lines: My lord?

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: Messala.

speeches.speaker: MESSALA
lines: What says my General?

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: Messala,
This is my birth-day; as this very day
Was Cassius born. Give me thy hand, Messala:
Be thou my witness that against my will
As Pompey was, am I compell’d to set
Upon one battle all our liberties.
You know that I held Epicurus strong,
And his opinion. Now I change my mind,
And partly credit things that do presage.
Coming from Sardis, on our former ensign
Two mighty eagles fell, and there they perch’d,
Gorging and feeding from our soldiers’ hands,
Who to Philippi here consorted us.
This morning are they fled away and gone,
And in their steads do ravens, crows, and kites
Fly o’er our heads, and downward look on us,
As we were sickly prey: their shadows seem
A canopy most fatal, under which
Our army lies, ready to give up the ghost.

speeches.speaker: MESSALA
lines: Believe not so.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: I but believe it partly,
For I am fresh of spirit, and resolv’d
To meet all perils very constantly.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Even so, Lucilius.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: Now, most noble Brutus,
The gods today stand friendly, that we may,
Lovers in peace, lead on our days to age!
But, since the affairs of men rest still incertain,
Let’s reason with the worst that may befall.
If we do lose this battle, then is this
The very last time we shall speak together:
What are you then determined to do?

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Even by the rule of that philosophy
By which I did blame Cato for the death
Which he did give himself, I know not how,
But I do find it cowardly and vile,
For fear of what might fall, so to prevent
The time of life, arming myself with patience
To stay the providence of some high powers
That govern us below.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: Then, if we lose this battle,
You are contented to be led in triumph
Thorough the streets of Rome?

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: No, Cassius, no: think not, thou noble Roman,
That ever Brutus will go bound to Rome;
He bears too great a mind. But this same day
Must end that work the Ides of March begun;
And whether we shall meet again I know not.
Therefore our everlasting farewell take.
For ever, and for ever, farewell, Cassius.
If we do meet again, why, we shall smile;
If not, why then this parting was well made.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: For ever and for ever farewell, Brutus.
If we do meet again, we’ll smile indeed;
If not, ’tis true this parting was well made.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Why then, lead on. O, that a man might know
The end of this day’s business ere it come!
But it sufficeth that the day will end,
And then the end is known. Come, ho! away!

scenes.setting: The same. The field of battle

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Ride, ride, Messala, ride, and give these bills
Unto the legions on the other side.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: O, look, Titinius, look, the villains fly!
Myself have to mine own turn’d enemy:
This ensign here of mine was turning back;
I slew the coward, and did take it from him.

speeches.speaker: TITINIUS
lines: O Cassius, Brutus gave the word too early,
Who, having some advantage on Octavius,
Took it too eagerly: his soldiers fell to spoil,
Whilst we by Antony are all enclos’d.

speeches.speaker: PINDARUS
lines: Fly further off, my lord, fly further off;
Mark Antony is in your tents, my lord.
Fly, therefore, noble Cassius, fly far off.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: This hill is far enough. Look, look, Titinius;
Are those my tents where I perceive the fire?

speeches.speaker: TITINIUS
lines: They are, my lord.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: Titinius, if thou lovest me,
Mount thou my horse and hide thy spurs in him,
Till he have brought thee up to yonder troops
And here again, that I may rest assur’d
Whether yond troops are friend or enemy.

speeches.speaker: TITINIUS
lines: I will be here again, even with a thought.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: Go, Pindarus, get higher on that hill,
My sight was ever thick. Regard Titinius,
And tell me what thou notest about the field.

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: What news?

speeches.speaker: PINDARUS
lines: With horsemen, that make to him on the spur,
Yet he spurs on. Now they are almost on him.
Now, Titinius! Now some light. O, he lights too.
He’s ta’en!

speeches.speaker: CASSIUS
lines: Come down; behold no more.
O, coward that I am, to live so long,
To see my best friend ta’en before my face!

speeches.speaker: PINDARUS
lines: So, I am free, yet would not so have been,
Durst I have done my will. O Cassius!
Far from this country Pindarus shall run,
Where never Roman shall take note of him.

speeches.speaker: MESSALA
lines: It is but change, Titinius; for Octavius
Is overthrown by noble Brutus’ power,
As Cassius’ legions are by Antony.

speeches.speaker: TITINIUS
lines: These tidings would well comfort Cassius.

speeches.speaker: MESSALA
lines: Where did you leave him?

speeches.speaker: TITINIUS
lines: All disconsolate,
With Pindarus his bondman, on this hill.

speeches.speaker: MESSALA
lines: Is not that he that lies upon the ground?

speeches.speaker: TITINIUS
lines: He lies not like the living. O my heart!

speeches.speaker: MESSALA
lines: Is not that he?

speeches.speaker: TITINIUS
lines: No, this was he, Messala,
But Cassius is no more. O setting sun,
As in thy red rays thou dost sink to night,
So in his red blood Cassius’ day is set.
The sun of Rome is set. Our day is gone;
Clouds, dews, and dangers come; our deeds are done.
Mistrust of my success hath done this deed.

speeches.speaker: MESSALA
lines: Mistrust of good success hath done this deed.
O hateful Error, Melancholy’s child!
Why dost thou show to the apt thoughts of men
The things that are not? O Error, soon conceiv’d,
Thou never com’st unto a happy birth,
But kill’st the mother that engender’d thee!

speeches.speaker: TITINIUS
lines: What, Pindarus! where art thou, Pindarus?

speeches.speaker: MESSALA
lines: Seek him, Titinius, whilst I go to meet
The noble Brutus, thrusting this report
Into his ears. I may say thrusting it;
For piercing steel and darts envenomed
Shall be as welcome to the ears of Brutus
As tidings of this sight.

speeches.speaker: TITINIUS
lines: Hie you, Messala,
And I will seek for Pindarus the while.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Where, where, Messala, doth his body lie?

speeches.speaker: MESSALA
lines: Lo, yonder, and Titinius mourning it.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Titinius’ face is upward.

speeches.speaker: CATO
lines: He is slain.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: O Julius Caesar, thou art mighty yet!
Thy spirit walks abroad, and turns our swords
In our own proper entrails.

speeches.speaker: CATO
lines: Brave Titinius!
Look whether he have not crown’d dead Cassius!

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Are yet two Romans living such as these?
The last of all the Romans, fare thee well!
It is impossible that ever Rome
Should breed thy fellow. Friends, I owe more tears
To this dead man than you shall see me pay.
I shall find time, Cassius, I shall find time.
Come therefore, and to Thassos send his body.
His funerals shall not be in our camp,
Lest it discomfort us. Lucilius, come;
And come, young Cato; let us to the field.
Labeo and Flavius, set our battles on.
’Tis three o’clock; and Romans, yet ere night
We shall try fortune in a second fight.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Yet, countrymen, O, yet hold up your heads!

speeches.speaker: CATO
lines: What bastard doth not? Who will go with me?
I will proclaim my name about the field.
I am the son of Marcus Cato, ho!
A foe to tyrants, and my country’s friend.
I am the son of Marcus Cato, ho!

speeches.speaker: LUCILIUS
lines: And I am Brutus, Marcus Brutus, I;
Brutus, my country’s friend; know me for Brutus!

speeches.stage: [_Exit, charging the enemy. Cato is overpowered, and falls._]

speeches.speaker: LUCILIUS
lines: O young and noble Cato, art thou down?
Why, now thou diest as bravely as Titinius,
And mayst be honour’d, being Cato’s son.

speeches.speaker: FIRST SOLDIER
lines: Yield, or thou diest.

speeches.speaker: LUCILIUS
lines: Only I yield to die:
There is so much that thou wilt kill me straight;

speeches.speaker: FIRST SOLDIER
lines: We must not. A noble prisoner!

speeches.speaker: SECOND SOLDIER
lines: Room, ho! Tell Antony, Brutus is ta’en.

speeches.speaker: FIRST SOLDIER
lines: I’ll tell the news. Here comes the General.

speeches.speaker: ANTONY
lines: Where is he?

speeches.speaker: LUCILIUS
lines: Safe, Antony; Brutus is safe enough.
I dare assure thee that no enemy
Shall ever take alive the noble Brutus.
The gods defend him from so great a shame!
When you do find him, or alive or dead,
He will be found like Brutus, like himself.

speeches.speaker: ANTONY
lines: This is not Brutus, friend; but, I assure you,
A prize no less in worth. Keep this man safe,
Give him all kindness. I had rather have
Such men my friends than enemies. Go on,
And see whether Brutus be alive or dead;
And bring us word unto Octavius’ tent
How everything is chanc’d.

speeches.stage: Enter Brutus, Dardanius, Clitus, Strato and Volumnius.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Come, poor remains of friends, rest on this rock.

speeches.speaker: CLITUS
lines: Statilius show’d the torch-light; but, my lord,
He came not back: he is or ta’en or slain.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Sit thee down, Clitus. Slaying is the word;
It is a deed in fashion. Hark thee, Clitus.

speeches.speaker: CLITUS
lines: What, I, my lord? No, not for all the world.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Peace then, no words.

speeches.speaker: CLITUS
lines: I’ll rather kill myself.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Hark thee, Dardanius.

speeches.speaker: DARDANIUS
lines: Shall I do such a deed?

speeches.speaker: CLITUS
lines: O Dardanius!

speeches.speaker: DARDANIUS
lines: O Clitus!

speeches.speaker: CLITUS
lines: What ill request did Brutus make to thee?

speeches.speaker: DARDANIUS
lines: To kill him, Clitus. Look, he meditates.

speeches.speaker: CLITUS
lines: Now is that noble vessel full of grief,
That it runs over even at his eyes.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Come hither, good Volumnius; list a word.

speeches.speaker: VOLUMNIUS
lines: What says my lord?

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Why, this, Volumnius:
The ghost of Caesar hath appear’d to me
Two several times by night; at Sardis once,
And this last night here in Philippi fields.
I know my hour is come.

speeches.speaker: VOLUMNIUS
lines: Not so, my lord.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Nay I am sure it is, Volumnius.
Thou seest the world, Volumnius, how it goes;
Our enemies have beat us to the pit.

speeches.speaker: VOLUMNIUS
lines: That’s not an office for a friend, my lord.

speeches.speaker: CLITUS
lines: Fly, fly, my lord! there is no tarrying here.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Farewell to you; and you; and you, Volumnius.
Strato, thou hast been all this while asleep;
Farewell to thee too, Strato.—Countrymen,
My heart doth joy, that yet in all my life
I found no man but he was true to me.
I shall have glory by this losing day
More than Octavius and Mark Antony
By this vile conquest shall attain unto.
So fare you well at once; for Brutus’ tongue
Hath almost ended his life’s history.
Night hangs upon mine eyes; my bones would rest,
That have but labour’d to attain this hour.

speeches.speaker: CLITUS
lines: Fly, my lord, fly!

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Hence! I will follow.

speeches.speaker: STRATO
lines: Give me your hand first. Fare you well, my lord.

speeches.speaker: BRUTUS
lines: Farewell, good Strato.—Caesar, now be still:
I kill’d not thee with half so good a will.

speeches.stage: [_He runs on his sword, and dies._]

speeches.speaker: OCTAVIUS
lines: What man is that?

speeches.speaker: MESSALA
lines: My master’s man. Strato, where is thy master?

speeches.speaker: STRATO
lines: Free from the bondage you are in, Messala.
The conquerors can but make a fire of him;
For Brutus only overcame himself,
And no man else hath honour by his death.

speeches.speaker: LUCILIUS
lines: So Brutus should be found. I thank thee, Brutus,
That thou hast prov’d Lucilius’ saying true.

speeches.speaker: OCTAVIUS
lines: All that serv’d Brutus, I will entertain them.
Fellow, wilt thou bestow thy time with me?

speeches.speaker: STRATO
lines: Ay, if Messala will prefer me to you.

speeches.speaker: OCTAVIUS
lines: Do so, good Messala.

speeches.speaker: MESSALA
lines: How died my master, Strato?

speeches.speaker: STRATO
lines: I held the sword, and he did run on it.

speeches.speaker: MESSALA
lines: Octavius, then take him to follow thee,
That did the latest service to my master.

speeches.speaker: ANTONY
lines: This was the noblest Roman of them all.
All the conspirators save only he,
Did that they did in envy of great Caesar;
He only, in a general honest thought
And common good to all, made one of them.
His life was gentle, and the elements
So mix’d in him that Nature might stand up
And say to all the world, “This was a man!”

speeches.speaker: OCTAVIUS
lines: According to his virtue let us use him
With all respect and rites of burial.
Within my tent his bones tonight shall lie,
Most like a soldier, order’d honourably.
So call the field to rest, and let’s away,
To part the glories of this happy day.
